title: Model: Human Body Systems Working Together

opener.title: Model: Human Body Systems Working Together
opener.question: When you need more energy, like during a race, how do your body systems team up to deliver it?
opener.alt: An opening film that follows one breath: from Earth's thin blue air seen from space, to two people breathing out on a cold day, to a cast of real human lungs, to tiny air sacs, to a red blood cell inside a tiny blood vessel, and finally to red blood cells under a microscope.

frames.label: Earth's air, seen from the space station
frames.scale: the blue layer is less than 100 km thick
frames.line: Every breath you take comes from this thin blue layer of air.

frames.label: Breathing out on a cold day
frames.line: On a cold day you can see a breath. Your lungs pull air in and push it back out all day long.

frames.label: A cast of real human lungs, in a museum
frames.line: Colored plastic fills the air tubes and the blood vessels. They branch again and again, side by side.

frames.label: An air sac and a tiny blood vessel (a model)
frames.scale: each air sac about 0.2 mm across
frames.line: At the end of the smallest air tubes, oxygen moves out of the air and into the blood.

frames.label: A red blood cell inside a capillary
frames.scale: electron microscope · the capillary is about 0.008 mm wide
frames.line: The thinnest blood vessels are so narrow that red blood cells pass through one at a time.

frames.label: Red blood cells
frames.scale: electron microscope · each one about 0.008 mm across
frames.line: Each red blood cell carries oxygen. An adult has about 25 trillion of them.

k-warmup.text: Put two fingers on the side of your neck and feel your pulse. Now guess: how fast will it beat after one minute of jumping jacks? Tap the heart in that rhythm. Then tap Save my beat and write why.

k-words.text: Body system. Respiratory system. Circulatory system. Digestive system. Muscular system. Pulse.

k-part1.text: In sixteen twenty-eight, William Harvey used math to study the heart. Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English. Then run the clock below and see how much blood one heart pushes out in half an hour.

k-quiz.text: Three quick questions, just for you. They are not graded. Tap an answer and read the note under it. Think about which organs work as a team.

k-assign.text: Now add your half of page nineteen. Answer the two Part B questions. In Part C, write your notebook page and use your pulse card. Then tap evidence cards in the planner to build your C-E-R about how your body systems team up.

beat.title: Tap the beat
beat.intro: Now imagine one minute of jumping jacks. How fast will your heart beat right after?
job: Tap the heart in the rhythm you think it will beat.
Keep tapping until a number shows.
Use −5 or +5 to fix it, then tap Save my beat.
beat.tapLabel: The heart. Tap it in the rhythm of your guess.
beat.notYet: Tap the heart at least four times in a steady rhythm.
beat.keepTapping: Keep tapping in a steady rhythm.
beat.tooLow: That is slower than most people's hearts beat while sitting still. Is that what you expect after jumping jacks?
beat.tooHigh: That is faster than almost any heart can beat. Try a slower rhythm.
beat.got: Got it. Tap Save my beat when it feels right.
beat.saved: 🔒 Saved: {n} beats per minute. You will check it with your real pulse in Part 4.
beat.lockedNote: 🔒 Your guess: {n} beats per minute. Part 4 shows your real pulse next to it.
beat.reasonPrompt: Why do you think so? Write at least 2 sentences. Which body systems are working together?
beat.placeholder: I think my heart will beat about ___ times a minute because…
beat.credit: Heart picture (a model): Patrick J. Lynch, medical illustrator (CC BY 2.5).

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to see what it means.

words.def: A team of organs that work together to do one big job.
Nose, windpipe, and lungs. It brings oxygen in and sends carbon dioxide out.
Heart, blood vessels, and blood. It carries oxygen and nutrients all over your body.
Mouth, stomach, and intestines. It breaks food down into nutrients your body can use.
The muscles that move your body. They need oxygen and nutrients to work.
The beat you feel when your heart pushes blood. You can count it at your wrist or neck.

source.title: Harvey does the math
source.alt: Two printed pages from William Harvey's 1628 book, pages 43 and 44, in Latin. The left page starts with the heading Caput IX, which means Chapter 9.
source.intro: These are pages 43 and 44 of Harvey's 1628 book, the same book as in the last lesson. In Chapter 9 he tried something new for his time: he used numbers to test an idea about the body.
job: Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English.
Then find the two lines in the hunts.

lines.en: Chapter 9. The blood goes around in a circle. Here is the proof.
First: the heartbeat pushes blood from the veins into the arteries without stopping, so much that the food we eat could never make it all.
Let us guess that each heartbeat in a person pushes out half an ounce, or three drams, or just one dram of blood. The valves will not let it flow back into the heart.
In half an hour, the heart beats more than a thousand times. In some people, and at some times, two, three, or even four thousand.

Multiply, and you will see that in half an hour, a thousand times three drams, or two drams, or five hundred ounces of blood pass through the heart into the arteries. That is always more blood than the whole body holds.
Even if it took an hour, or a whole day, more blood passes through the heart than food could ever make, or than the veins could hold at one time.

asks.q: Hunt 1: Find the line that says how many times the heart beats in half an hour.
asks.yes: Yes. More than a thousand beats in half an hour. You will use that number in the clock below.
asks.no: Not that one. Look near the bottom of the left page.

asks.q: Hunt 2: Find the line where Harvey says this is more blood than the whole body holds.
asks.yes: Yes. More blood than the whole body! Now run the clock and see it for yourself.
asks.no: Not quite. Look at the top of the right page.

source.credit: Source: William Harvey, De motu cordis (Frankfurt, 1628), Chapter 9, pages 43 and 44, from the 1928 facsimile (Internet Archive, public domain in the U.S.). Plain-English version written for this lesson.

clock.title: Run the clock
clock.intro: Harvey guessed how much blood one heartbeat pushes out, then counted the beats in half an hour. Try his numbers.
job: Pick how much blood one beat pushes out.
Pick how many beats happen in half an hour.
Tap Run the clock, or drag the clock hand around.
clock.amtQ: 1. How much blood does one beat push out?

amounts.sub: about 4 mL, less than a teaspoon
about 12 mL, a little less than a tablespoon

clock.beatsQ: 2. How many beats in half an hour?

beatsOpts.sub: a resting adult heart, about 70 a minute

clock.bodyLabel: Thick lines = about {n} liters, all the blood in an adult's body
clock.pastLabel: more than a whole body's blood!
clock.pickFirst: First pick how much blood one beat pushes out.
clock.faceLabel: Clock hand. Drag it around, or use the arrow keys, to move through half an hour.
clock.clockAlt: A real wall clock by Aaron Willard, an American clockmaker. The clock face is in a wooden case.
clock.okPast: Half an hour of beats pushed out about {l} liters. That is more blood than a whole body holds!
clock.notPast: Only {l} liters, not past the line yet. But Harvey wrote more than a thousand beats. Try a real resting heart, or a bigger amount.
clock.today: Harvey kept his guesses small on purpose, to be safe. Today we know each beat of an adult heart pushes out about 70 mL. At 70 beats a minute, that is about 150 liters in half an hour, nearly enough to fill a bathtub.
clock.cupsAlt: Two real glass measuring cups. The big one on the right holds 1 liter.
clock.cupsCap: Each jug in the game holds 1 liter, like the big cup on the right. Photo: Picofluidicist (CC0).
clock.ask: Harvey asked: where could all that blood come from? What is the best answer?

opts.t: The body makes that much new blood from food every half hour
opts.hint: Harvey thought about that. You would need to eat and drink more than your own weight every hour. Try again.

opts.t: The same blood goes out from the heart and comes back to it, around and around
The muscles use the blood up, and it disappears
opts.hint: Then where would 150 liters every half hour come from? Remember Harvey's vein test: blood in the veins flows back toward the heart.

clock.win: Yes. That is Harvey's big idea: the blood travels in a circle, over and over.
clock.wow: At rest, all the blood in your body makes one full trip around in about one minute. During a hard run, it can go around four or five times faster.
clock.why: A dram was a small unit of weight that doctors and druggists used in Harvey's time. Eight drams made one ounce. One dram of blood is about 4 milliliters.
clock.credit: Numbers: Harvey (1628), Chapter 9. Today: about 70 mL per beat at rest, and about 5 liters of blood in an adult. Clock: Aaron Willard, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (CC0).

brain.name: Brain
brain.job: Thinks, feels, and sends messages to the body

eyes.name: Eyes
eyes.job: Sense organs: see light, shapes, and colors

heart.name: Heart
heart.job: Pumps blood to every part of the body

lungs.name: Lungs
lungs.job: Take in oxygen and push out carbon dioxide

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.job: Mashes food and mixes it with juices

intestines.name: Intestines
intestines.job: Finish breaking down food and pass nutrients and water into the blood

liver.name: Liver
liver.job: Cleans the blood and makes bile that helps digest fat

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.job: Makes digestive juices and helps control sugar in the blood

kidneys.name: Kidneys
kidneys.job: Filter waste and extra water out of the blood

bladder.name: Bladder
bladder.job: Stores urine until you go to the bathroom

skin.name: Skin
skin.job: Keeps germs out, senses touch and heat, sweats to cool you

muscles.name: Muscles
muscles.job: Pull on bones to move you

skeleton.name: Skeleton
skeleton.job: Holds you up. The skull protects the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs

gauge.title: Keep the gauges up
gauge.intro: The runner just finished a sprint and sat down. You control two members of the team: the heart and the lungs. Give the muscles just the oxygen they need.
job: Pick what the runner is doing.
Slide the heartbeat and the breathing.
Keep the oxygen bar in the green for 3 seconds.

acts.win: Sitting needs only a calm heart and slow breathing.
Walking needs a little more of both.
Sprinting needs a fast heart and fast breathing, both at once.

gauge.msgOk: The heart and lungs are keeping up. Hold it there.
gauge.msgLowBr: The heart is pumping fast, but the blood has too little fresh oxygen to carry. Speed up the breathing.
gauge.msgLowHr: The lungs pull in plenty of air, but the blood moves too slowly to deliver it. Speed up the heart.
gauge.msgLow: Both are too slow for this. The muscles are running low on oxygen.
gauge.msgWaste: That is faster than this needs. Your body speeds up only as much as the muscles need.

jar.title: Breathe out: what is left?
jar.intro: Each jar shows 100 tiny bits of air. Air you breathe in has 21 oxygen bits (blue). How many are left in the air you breathe out?
jar.guessLabel: My guess, oxygen bits left in 100 bits of breath:
jar.guessFirst: Slide to make your guess first.
jar.winLow: You guessed {g}. Many people think a breath out has almost no oxygen left. But it still has about 16 oxygen bits in every 100! Your body takes only about a quarter of the oxygen. The orange bits are carbon dioxide, the waste your blood brought back from your muscles.
jar.win: You guessed {g}. A breath out still has about 16 oxygen bits in every 100. Your body takes only about a quarter of the oxygen. The orange bits are carbon dioxide, the waste your blood brought back from your muscles.

gauge.whyTitle: Why do both have to speed up?
gauge.why: Oxygen gets into the blood in the lungs. The heart then pumps that blood to the muscles. If only the heart speeds up, the blood has too little fresh oxygen. If only the breathing speeds up, the oxygen waits in the lungs because the blood moves too slowly. The team works only when both speed up.
gauge.credit: Photo: Sgt. Jennifer Spradlin, U.S. Army (public domain). Organ pictures: Servier Medical Art (CC BY-SA 3.0). The game's numbers are a model. Air out is about 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide.

peek.kicker: Part 3 game · What the model leaves out
peek.title: Peek under the box
peek.intro: Move the magnifying lens over each box to see a real picture of what that box hides.
job: Drag the lens over a box, or tap a box.
Read what the model leaves out.

boxes.name: Lungs
boxes.alt: A microscope picture of lung tissue: many round, empty spaces with thin pink and purple walls.
boxes.text: Hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, each about 0.2 mm across. Their walls are so thin that oxygen passes right through them into the blood. The box shows none of this.
boxes.credit: Lung air sacs under a microscope: Yale Rosen (CC BY-SA 2.0).

boxes.name: Stomach and intestines
boxes.alt: Four drawings of tiny finger-like bumps from the inside of the small intestine, as seen through a microscope.
boxes.text: The inside of the small intestine is covered with tiny fingers called villi. Nutrients from your food pass through them into the blood. This drawing comes from an old science book.
boxes.credit: The villi of the small intestine, Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0).

boxes.name: Heart and blood
boxes.alt: An electron microscope picture of many red blood cells, shaped like flat, dented disks, with two round, bumpy white blood cells.
boxes.text: Blood is full of cells. The flat, dented disks are red blood cells: they carry the oxygen. The two bumpy balls are white blood cells, which fight germs. One drop of blood holds hundreds of millions of red blood cells.
boxes.credit: Blood cells, scanning electron microscope: Bruce Wetzel and Harry Schaefer, National Cancer Institute (public domain).

boxes.name: Muscles
boxes.alt: A microscope picture of long pink muscle fibers, with a thin chain of tiny cells running between them.
boxes.text: Muscles are made of long fibers. Look for the thin chain of tiny cells running between them: that is a capillary, a blood vessel so narrow that red blood cells pass through one at a time. This is where oxygen and nutrients are dropped off.
boxes.credit: Skeletal muscle with a capillary: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library (CC0).

peek.ask: So, is a simple box-and-arrow model a bad model?

opts.t: Yes. A good model must show every cell.
opts.hint: A model with every cell would be too crowded to show the team. Think about what a model is for.

opts.t: No. It leaves out tiny parts on purpose, so you can see the whole team at once.
Yes. A model is only a guess, so it can't be useful.
opts.hint: Scientists and doctors use models every day to explain and to predict. Is that useless?

peek.win: Right. A good model shows the big idea and is honest about what it leaves out: cells, tiny vessels, and how fast it all happens.
peek.credit: Box pictures: Servier Medical Art (CC BY-SA 3.0).

lab.intro: Collect real data from your own body, then build a model that explains it.
lab.title: The pulse lab
lab.alt: One person presses two fingers on the inside of another person's wrist, just below the thumb, to feel the pulse.
lab.how: Press two fingers (not your thumb) on the inside of your wrist, just below your thumb. Or use the side of your neck, under your jaw. Press gently until you feel the beat.
lab.safe: If you have a health reason not to exercise, march slowly in place or move your arms instead. You can still collect data.
lab.credit: Photo: Staff Sgt. Jeanette Copeland, U.S. Air Force (public domain).

steps.text: Sit still for one minute. Tap Start, then tap the red button for each beat or breath you feel. Or count by yourself and type the number.
Do jumping jacks or march fast in place for one full minute. If you can't do jumping jacks, do fast arm circles.
As soon as you stop, count again the same way.

lab.moveDone: ✓ One minute done. Measure right away!
lab.odd: One of your numbers looks unusual. Count again carefully, or type the number you counted.
lab.noRise: Your pulse did not go up. Did you move for the whole minute and measure right away? You can measure again.
lab.win: Your heart went from {a} to {b} beats per minute: {d} more beats every minute! Now load the arrows in your model below.

cargo.title: Load the arrows
cargo.intro: Each arrow carries something from one system to another. Load each arrow with the right cargo.
job: Tap a cargo tag, then tap an arrow. Or drag the tag onto the arrow.

arrows.hint: What does the air in your lungs give to the blood?

wrong.co2: Carbon dioxide goes the other way: from the blood into the lungs, and out with your breath.
wrong.food: Nutrients come from food, not from the air in your lungs.
wrong.sig: Signals come from the brain, not the lungs.

arrows.hint: What does your digestive system get out of food?

wrong.o2: The stomach and intestines don't take in air. What do they get from food?
wrong.co2: This arrow carries something useful from your food into the blood.
wrong.sig: Signals come from the brain, not the stomach.

arrows.hint: The blood delivers two things the working muscles need.
arrows.more: Good start. This arrow carries two things. What else do muscles need?

wrong.co2: Carbon dioxide is the muscles' waste. Which way does waste travel?
wrong.sig: Signals come from the brain, not the blood.

arrows.hint: Working muscles make a waste gas. The blood carries it away.

wrong.o2: Muscles use up oxygen. What do they send back?
wrong.food: Muscles use up nutrients. What waste do they send back?
wrong.sig: Muscles don't send signals into the blood.

arrows.hint: How does the waste gas leave your body?

wrong.o2: The lungs give oxygen to the blood, not the other way. What does the blood drop off at the lungs?
wrong.food: Nutrients go to the cells, not out of the lungs.

arrows.hint: How does the brain tell the muscles to move faster?

wrong.o2: The brain doesn't send oxygen. It sends messages.
wrong.food: The brain doesn't send nutrients. It sends messages.
wrong.co2: The brain doesn't send waste to the muscles. It sends messages.

cargo.wrongHint: Not quite. Think about where that cargo comes from and where it goes.
cargo.pickTag: First tap a cargo tag above, then tap this arrow.
cargo.win: Your model works. Oxygen and nutrients come in, the heart and blood deliver them, the muscles use them, and carbon dioxide goes back out. The brain keeps the team in step.
cargo.upYes: I guessed faster than at rest
cargo.upNo: I guessed about the same or slower
cargo.evFlat: It did not go up (measure again)

twist.head: Harvey's model had a hole in it.
twist.line: Harvey showed that blood goes out through the arteries and comes back through the veins. But he never saw how it got from one to the other. Those vessels were too small to see.
twist.chain: In 1661, four years after Harvey died, Marcello Malpighi looked at a frog's lung through a microscope. He found the missing link: capillaries, the tiny vessels you peeked at in Part 3. A better tool filled the gap in the model.

chain.what: Where does a tree come from?
Can a plant fix the air?
How do we draw the path of energy?
Where does all that blood go?
How do structures help living things survive?

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: After one minute of exercise, my heart beat faster and I breathed faster at the same time.
In Keep the gauges up, speeding up only the heart or only the breathing did not keep the muscles in the green. Both had to speed up.
The lungs send oxygen into the blood, and the heart pumps that blood to the muscles.
Nutrients from the small intestine go into the blood, and the blood carries them to the muscles.
The blood carries carbon dioxide from the muscles back to the lungs, and I breathe it out.
Harvey's math showed that the same blood goes around and around, about one full trip each minute at rest.

checklist: Warm-Up: your beat guess and two sentences of reasons.
Part 4: your pulse data, at rest and after moving.
Part B: questions 1 and 2, in complete sentences.
Part C: your notebook page (both boxes).
C-E-R: a claim, your pulse data and at least one arrow from your model, and your reasoning.

Your pulse table and your loaded model (Part 4)

footage.title: Running on a treadmill in space
footage.intro: On the International Space Station, nothing pulls you down, so the heart and muscles barely have to work. Astronauts exercise about two hours every day to keep them strong. Watch an astronaut strap into a harness that holds him on the treadmill.
look: The video is sped up. Watch the astronaut float in and put on the harness.
Find the stretchy cords that pull him down onto the treadmill.
Why would a heart get weaker if it never had to work hard?
footage.credit: Video: “SpeedyTime: Treadmill 2,” NASA Johnson Space Center (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons. Cut, sped up, and muted for this lesson.

data.title: Resting heartbeats, from babies to grandparents
data.unit: beats per minute (the middle value for that age group)
data.intro: Government scientists measured the resting pulse of thousands of people in the United States, from babies to grandparents. Each bar shows the middle value for one age group, in years.
job: Drag across the bars to read each number.

opts.t: Babies have the fastest resting heartbeats, and the beat slows down as children grow
Resting heartbeats get faster as people grow up
opts.hint: Read the first bar, then the last. Which one is taller?

opts.t: Everyone's resting heart beats about the same
opts.hint: Compare 126 for babies with 69 for people 60 to 79. Are those close?

data.win: Babies have the fastest resting heartbeats, about 126 a minute. The beat slows as children grow, then stays about the same in grown-ups, about 70. Most 9 to 11 year olds rest at about 81.
data.alt: A bar graph of resting heartbeats per minute by age: under 1 year 126, ages 2 to 3 105, 4 to 5 94, 6 to 8 85, 9 to 11 81, 12 to 15 76, 16 to 19 73, 20 to 39 71, 60 to 79 69.
data.credit: Data: Ostchega and others, “Resting Pulse Rate Reference Data for Children, Adolescents, and Adults: United States, 1999–2008,” National Health Statistics Reports No. 41 (CDC, August 2011), Table 1, 50th percentile. Downloaded 24 Nov 2026.

cabinet.title: Olympic ski boots from 1988
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of two hard plastic ski boots, yellow and black, with metal buckles.
cabinet.text: These are real ski boots worn by Seba Johnson. In 1988, when she was 14, she raced at the Winter Olympics in Calgary, Canada, for the U.S. Virgin Islands. She was the youngest alpine ski racer in Olympic history and the first Black woman to ski in the Olympics. Ski races start high on mountains, where each breath brings in less oxygen, so a racer's heart and lungs work extra hard.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Ski boots worn by Seba Johnson, National Museum of African American History and Culture, Smithsonian (CC0).
